source: Ghosal et al. (2025, NeurIPS) Does Thinking More Always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models
finding: Appending 'Wait' or 'think more' to extend one trace helps at first, then hurts. At the same token budget, several independent traces plus a vote beat the extended single trace.
numbers: Accuracy rose 82.2% to 87.3% as thinking grew 385 to 1100 tokens, then fell to 70.3% at 15980 tokens. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on GSM8K: Wait out to 16000 tokens gave -11.8% vs standard thinking, parallel at the same budget gave +10.1%. At a 16K budget parallel was about 22% and 47% higher than Wait-and-Think-More and exact-length thinking. Three distilled models, GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME 2024.
quote: Parallel thinking consistently maintains or enhances accuracy with increasing thinking budget.
limits: Small distilled R1 models. The sequential arm is a blind 'Wait' loop, not a conflict cue fired by a check. Parallel selection uses a likelihood-based self-reward over agreeing answers. Authors' own method. Does not test a gated cue.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a blind second look is not free. Any conflict cue must beat a plain second sample at equal tokens, and the default prior from this paper is that independent samples win. Gate the cue on a real signal.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Forcing the model to keep going by appending 'Wait' improved s1-32B a little. The authors report that majority voting on the base model could not catch up, but that comparison is across different models, not equal tokens.
numbers: s1 without forcing / Wait 1x / 2x / 4x: AIME24 50.0 / 53.3 / 53.3 / 56.7; MATH500 92.6 / 92.8 / 93.0 / 92.2; GPQA-Diamond 56.6 / 59.6 / 59.6 / 58.6. Text: AIME24 from 50% to 57% with budget forcing. Too many forced continuations can cause repetitive loops. Base Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct majority voting over 2 to 64 samples was plotted against s1-32B.
quote: Scaling test-time compute on the base model via majority voting cannot catch up with the performance of s1-32B
limits: Compares a fine-tuned model with budget forcing to an untuned base with voting, so it does not isolate the cue. Gains of 3 to 7 points on 30-question AIME are noisy. Ghosal 2025 reaches the opposite ranking at equal tokens on other models.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the pro-cue evidence is confounded and the anti-cue evidence (Ghosal) is from small distilled models. Contested; no clean test on frontier models.

source: Fu, Wang, Tian, Zhao (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: A token-level confidence signal (mean log-prob confidence, lowest 2,048-token group, tail confidence) picks out bad traces. Dropping low-confidence traces during generation saves tokens at equal or better accuracy. Confidence is an inner signal that predicts a wrong trace.
numbers: Offline, 512 traces: GPT-OSS-120B AIME25 pass@1 91.8, majority 97.0, DeepConf 99.9. DeepSeek-8B AIME25 82.3 to 87.4. Qwen3-32B AIME24 85.3 to 90.8. Lowest-group-confidence filtering (top 10%), DeepSeek-8B: +0.26 to +9.38 pp over best voting (mean +5.27). Online: up to 84.7% fewer tokens at equal or better accuracy. Averaged over 64 repetitions, five benchmarks, five open models.
quote: it can sometimes hurt performance due to model overconfidence on incorrect problems
limits: Open-weight models with logprob access; math and GPQA only. Keeping the top 10% hurt GPT-OSS-120B on some sets (HMMT25 92.9 to 88.9). Measures trace quality, not 'wrong frame' as such.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 1: a token-confidence trigger with a measured gain at lower token cost is the one signal here with compute-fair evidence. Warns that confident-wrong traces escape it.

source: Tsui (2026, COLM) Self-Correction Bench v3, section 4.4 reasoning models
finding: Reasoning models show a small or even negative self-correction blind spot, unlike the 14 non-reasoning models (64.5%). Appending 'Wait' to a non-thinking base model gets close to its reasoning sibling.
numbers: Table 3 macro accuracy, base / base+Wait / reasoning: DeepSeek-V3-0324 vs R1-0528 0.567 / 0.902 / 0.908; phi-4 0.325 / 0.701 / 0.707; Qwen3-14B 0.117 / 0.868 / 0.843; Qwen3-32B 0.045 / 0.793 / 0.894; Qwen3-30B-A3B 0.104 / 0.860 / 0.845; Qwen3-235B-A22B 0.328 / 0.856 / 0.876. Qwen3 non-thinking mode still shows the blind spot.
quote: Reasoning models exhibit a small, even negative, Self-Correction Blind Spot
limits: Open models only (R1, Qwen3, phi-4-reasoning-plus, QwQ). Errors are injected and benchmark tasks are synthetic. No Claude, GPT-5 or Gemini reasoning models in the tables I read.
agent_relevance: Gap 4, partly closed: the blind spot belongs to non-reasoning mode. For a thinking-mode agent the cue that matters is for errors that survive a whole trace, not injected local ones.

source: Petrova & Vejsiu (2026) Spectral Origins of the Self-Correction Blind Spot in Autoregressive Generation
finding: Theory paper. Claims the blind spot occurs if and only if a spectral radius of the error-propagation operator is at least one, and that the 'Wait' effect (89.3%) is recovered by a threshold. Only the abstract was read.
numbers: Restates the 89.3% 'Wait' reduction from Tsui; no new LLM experiment seen in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Theory, not a replication. Not independent evidence for the effect size.
agent_relevance: Low weight; do not count as a second source for K13.

source: Mehta (2026) Confident and Wrong: Silent Semantic Failures in Coding Agents
finding: Coding agents often fail by committing to the same wrong reading of the task on every run. Submit rate and run-to-run consistency both look healthy while the answer is wrong. This is a measured case of a persistent wrong frame.
numbers: 1,750 trajectories, 50 SWE-bench Verified tasks, 4 models, 5 runs each. Submit vs resolve: GPT-5 100% vs 44%; Llama 4 99% vs 18%; Gemini 70% vs 50%. Silent semantic failure (5/5 submit, 0/5 resolve): 80% of Llama 4 failing runs, 68% of GPT-5 (19/50 tasks), 16% of Gemini (4/50). Patch embedding cosine across runs on silent-failure tasks 0.80 to 0.91 vs 0.48 to 0.57 baseline.
limits: One benchmark, one author, 50 tasks. Resolve is the hidden test, so it is an outcome label, not a live signal. 2025-era models.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 7: sample disagreement is the wrong conflict trigger when the frame itself is wrong, since all samples agree. Need an external check (test) or a frame-level contrast.

source: Mehta (2026) Confident and Wrong, sections 5.5 and 5.6: process signals and pre-edit guards
finding: Cheap test-free process signals catch some failures. Prompts that ask the agent to restate or check its reading before editing do not raise the resolve rate.
numbers: 3-gram loop detector (a command triple repeated 3 or more times) flagged 100% of Gemini's 0/5 no-submit tasks, no false positives on Claude or GPT-5; step ceiling over 245 steps caught 80%. Shorter trajectories predict silent failure (r=-0.26, p<0.001); phase-mix entropy r=+0.20, p<0.01. Guards: Claude 65.2% to 64.8%; GPT-5 44.4% to 46.0% (interpretation guard) and 44.4% to 44.0% (test-anchored guard); test-anchored guard cut GPT-5 silent failures from 19/50 to 16/50, helped astropy +4, django +6, matplotlib +6 pp, hurt scikit-learn -10, sympy -8.
limits: Loop detector catches abstention loops, not committed wrong fixes. Correlations are weak (r 0.2 to 0.26). Only 2 prompt types tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: first measured numbers on a repeated-call trigger (detects stalls only) and a clear negative on 'reread your reading' prompts. Supports an external check over self-reinterpretation.

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, tables 5 and 6 (feedback prompt variants)
finding: The default review prompt was already neutral ('could be either correct or incorrect'), and accuracy still fell. Three different review wordings all failed to beat the first answer. Wording moved CommonSenseQA results by several points, so phrasing matters, but no wording removed the loss.
numbers: GPT-4-Turbo: standard GSM8K 91.5, CSQA 84.0. Neutral prompt round 1/2: GSM8K 88.0/90.0, CSQA 81.5/83.0. 'Determine whether it is correct, if wrong find the problems': 90.0/90.0 and 74.5/81.0. 'Verify and explain': 91.0/91.0 and 81.5/83.5. Llama-2: standard 62.0 / 64.0; neutral GSM8K 43.5, 36.5, CSQA 37.5, 36.5; 'verify': GSM8K 58.0, 41.5, CSQA 24.0, 43.0. GPT-3.5 GSM8K: keeps first answer 74.7% of the time.
quote: Assume that this answer could be either correct or incorrect.
limits: 2023-era models, small test sets, accuracy only. The 'false options look relevant' explanation for CSQA is still untested. No reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Gaps 8 and 9: the untested hypothesis in K22 is partly answered. A neutral wording does not remove the loss on weak models, and an explanation-first wording was least harmful (91.0 vs 91.5 on GSM8K). Keep the adopt-only-if-check-improves rule.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
finding: Lessons distilled from both successes and failures raise success on later tasks, including across sites and domains. Memory built only from successes helps less, and one success-only baseline got worse when failures were added.
numbers: SWE-Bench-Verified resolve rate Gemini-2.5-flash 34.2 (no memory) to 38.8; Gemini-2.5-pro 54.0 to 57.4. Mind2Web cross-domain task SR (flash) 1.0 to 1.6, cross-task 3.3 to 4.8. WebArena Shopping with failures: ReasoningBank 46.5 (success only) to 49.7; Synapse 40.6 to 41.7; AWM 44.4 to 42.2. WebArena Multi subset +4.6 over the best baseline, where AWM fell below no-memory.
limits: Success and failure labels come from an LLM judge. Mind2Web task-SR gains are tiny in absolute terms (under 2 pp). Lessons are strategy-level, not 'assumption X was wrong' frame lessons. No direct different-type harm test.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: stored lessons transfer within and across sites, modestly. Failure lessons help only if written as general strategy. Harm is shown for AWM on cross-site tasks.

source: Ni et al. (2026) Trace2Skill: Distill Trajectory-Local Lessons into Transferable Agent Skills
finding: Skills built from many failure traces transfer across model size and to out-of-distribution tasks, but the same tables show negative cells, and a human-written skill that hurt a smaller agent.
numbers: Skills evolved from Qwen3.5-35B traces raised Qwen3.5-122B by up to +57.65 pp on WikiTableQuestions (error-derived skill, one cell). Same table row: -7.70 in another column; other rows show -6.36 and -5.83. The official xlsx skill helped a 122B agent and hurt the 35B agent on the same benchmark.
quote: broad, stale, or mismatched ones can distract or even hurt the agent
limits: Mixed-sign cells; the authors note high variance in single columns. Skills are SOP documents, not a single lesson from one solved impasse. Spreadsheet, table QA and math only.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: transfer works and harm exists. Store a lesson with its applicability condition and let code drop it when the task type does not match.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) Beyond Self-Reflection: An Execute-Distill-Verify Framework for Agentic Experience Learning (EDV)
finding: When an agent writes its own lesson after a failure, it may endorse its own mistake and store it (the Self-Confirmation Trap). A third-party distiller plus unanimous review cut the trap rate and raised held-out performance.
numbers: Self-Confirmation Trap Rate on an annotated Retail subset 11.0% (RB-MaTTS) to 5.0% (EDV). Held-out tau2-bench average Pass@1: No Memory 76.4, RB-MaTTS 81.1, EDV 85.1; EDV minus RB-MaTTS +4.0 Airline, +2.0 Retail, +5.8 Telecom (3 runs). Unanimous review can reject correct lessons.
limits: Same-domain held-out tasks only, not different-type tasks. Reviewers are models that may share the same error. Authors' own method.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 7: a lesson from a solved impasse needs a check by a different model or by code before it is stored, since a false insight can be stored as truth.

source: Liu et al. (2025, COLM) Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective
finding: 'Aha moment' self-reflection words already appear in base models (DeepSeek-V3-Base, Qwen2.5). In R1-Zero, responses with self-reflection were not more accurate than those without.
numbers: Checked on 500 MATH questions with keyword and LLM detection; the paper shows distributions and I did not extract a percentage. Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B reaches about 40% under several templates after RL.
quote: self-reflection does not necessarily imply higher accuracy
limits: Math only. Keyword detection is noisy. Plot-based; no table of rates read.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: a confident-looking mid-trace reversal is not evidence of a right new frame. Second source, with d'Aliberti, for treating an Aha as a claim to verify.

source: Ji et al. (2025) MathSticks: A Benchmark for Visual Symbolic Compositional Reasoning with Matchstick Puzzles
finding: Matchstick equations (move one or two sticks to fix a false equation) stay hard for strong reasoning models. Giving the equation as text, which repairs the input, raises accuracy at every level. No constraint-relaxation hint was tested.
numbers: 14 VLMs. With text / without text, L1 to L4 and average: o3 73, 56, 56, 55 (60.00) / 69, 37, 30, 18 (38.50); Gemini-2.5-Pro 45.25 / 22.50; Gemini-2.5-Flash 26.50 / 8.50; o4-mini 24.75 / 10.50; GPT-4o 0.00 / 0.00. Humans (3 adults, visual only) 91.72% average. 1.4M generated instances.
quote: Providing the equation string improves accuracy for all models
limits: Matchstick equations with strict stick conservation; difficulty is move count, not the Knoblich constraint classes. Only 3 humans. No hint variants.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 10: a missing-information fix (add the text) gave +21.5 pp for o3, so incomplete encoding is a real LLM failure type. The Knoblich Exp 3 analogue (tell the model which rule may bend) is still untested.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Six kinds of hint were placed in prompts. Models changed answers because of the hint but rarely said so in their chain of thought.
numbers: Average faithfulness (hint used and mentioned): Claude 3.7 Sonnet 25%, DeepSeek R1 39%. On misaligned hints: 20% and 29%. Outcome RL raises faithfulness then plateaus at 28% (MMLU) and 20% (GPQA).
quote: the reveal rate is often below 20%
limits: Hints are answer hints, not rule-relaxation hints. Tests faithfulness, not solve rate.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 analogy only: an LLM acts on an injected hint without reporting it, so a relaxation hint can change behaviour silently. Log which hints were given in code, not from the model's own account.

source: Wiley & Danek (2023) Restructuring processes and Aha! experiences in insight problem solving (Nature Reviews Psychology)
finding: Found by Crossref search as a recent review of restructuring. Full text blocked (login redirect), so I did not read what it says about cognitive conflict.
numbers: none read. Crossref: authors Wiley and Danek, 48 citations.
limits: Not opened. Cannot be used as evidence for or against a separate conflict step.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open; this is the first place to look for an independent view.

source: The Eyes as a Mirror of the Unconscious: pupil dilation and unconscious analytic thought in insight (J. Intelligence 14(9):211, 2026)
finding: Found by Crossref title search: a 2026 pupillometry paper on insight. The page returned HTTP 403, so I could not read design, N or results.
limits: Not opened; I cannot tell whether it separates conflict from restructuring.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the kind of timed design the cross-checker asked for may exist; open it before calling the gap real.
